Cardiovascular Disease

Acute Coronary Syndromes

ACS is a time-sensitive spectrum: unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI. The ED move is to combine symptom trajectory, ECG, troponin, risk features, and reperfusion eligibility without waiting for one test to solve the whole case.

Board trap: a single normal ECG or first troponin does not clear ACS. A patient can be pain-free with Wellens, have posterior/RV STEMI missed on standard leads, or have high-risk NSTEMI needing early invasive care.

Tintinalli separates unstable angina into rest angina, new-onset angina, and increasing angina. High-risk features include prolonged rest pain, pulmonary edema, new or worsening MR murmur, S3/rales, hypotension, bradycardia, tachycardia, dynamic ST changes, and elevated biomarkers. Rosen adds HEART score/pathway structure for low- and intermediate-risk ED disposition, but the score never replaces clinician concern for STEMI equivalents or unstable physiology.

ECG Localization and Culprit Artery

ECG localization is not decoration; it changes urgency, catheterization planning, and hemodynamic precautions. Inferior STEMI is II, III, and aVF. Anterior STEMI involves V1-V4; lateral involves I/aVL/V5-V6; true posterior MI appears as reciprocal anterior ST depression and needs posterior leads. Inferior STEMI plus V1 elevation should raise right ventricular infarction concern, where preload dependence makes nitrates dangerous.

Tintinalli's figures walk through the common STEMI maps: circumflex inferolateral MI, aVR elevation suggesting left main/proximal LAD disease, RCA inferior MI, RV infarction, distal and proximal LAD infarction, posterior MI, and right-sided RV leads. The tables and ECG strips belong together: first identify the ST territory, then ask what artery and complication pattern fits.

ECG Traps, Wellens, and Markers

ECG interpretation becomes difficult with early repolarization, LVH, LBBB, paced rhythm, pericarditis, myocarditis, hypothermia, digoxin effect, pulmonary disease, CNS catastrophe, and multiple cardiomyopathies. In LBBB or paced rhythms, concordant ST elevation/depression and excessive discordance are the dangerous patterns. Do not dismiss concordance as baseline bundle-branch noise.

Wellens syndrome is the classic pain-free trap: a patient may have resolved chest pain, normal or minimally elevated markers, and deep/biphasic anterior T waves that signal critical LAD disease. Stress testing these patients is dangerous; they need early invasive evaluation. Troponin is useful, but serial testing and ECG context remain central.

ED Treatment and Reperfusion

General treatment begins with rapid ECG, monitor, IV access, aspirin when not contraindicated, nitrates for pain/hypertension when safe, anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy, beta-blockade only when appropriate, and rapid reperfusion planning for STEMI. STEMI needs PCI when timely; fibrinolysis is considered when PCI delay is excessive and there are no contraindications.

Drug tables belong in the treatment section, not as an orphan dose appendix. Tintinalli lists STEMI and NSTEMI/UA drug options separately because fibrinolytics apply to STEMI reperfusion, while NSTEMI care uses risk-based antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and invasive strategies. Rosen's medication table reinforces the same ED classes while making indication and risk issues explicit.

Medication trap: right ventricular infarction plus hypotension is not the time for nitrates; possible dissection is not the time to reflexively load antithrombotics before considering the diagnosis.

Dysrhythmias and Mechanical Complications

Early ACS complications include bradyarrhythmias, AV block, sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation/flutter, accelerated idioventricular rhythm, VT, and VF. Treat the patient and hemodynamics, not just the rhythm strip. Temporary pacing is considered for symptomatic bradycardia or high-risk AV block that does not respond to atropine or is unlikely to remain stable.

Right ventricular infarction produces preload-sensitive shock and may accompany inferior MI. Mechanical complications are less common in the PCI era but remain deadly: free wall rupture, septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, pericarditis, heart failure, recurrent ischemia, and cardiogenic shock. Sudden decompensation after AMI should trigger echo, hemodynamic support, and urgent cardiology/cardiothoracic consultation.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. Rest angina lasting more than 20 minutes is classified as:

A. Stable anginaStable angina is predictable/exertional.
B. Unstable angina presentationCorrect.
C. Pericarditis onlyNot by definition.
D. Normal variantNo.

Q2. High-risk unstable angina feature:

A. Pulmonary edema or new/worsening MR murmurCorrect.
B. Pain only with palpationLow likelihood feature.
C. Normal ECG and normal markers onlyLow-risk pattern.
D. Age under 30 with no risk factorsLower risk.

Q3. ST elevation in II, III, and aVF localizes to:

A. AnteriorV1-V4.
B. LateralI/aVL/V5-V6.
C. Posterior onlyPosterior uses V7-V9 or reciprocal V1-V3 changes.
D. InferiorCorrect.

Q4. Posterior MI should be suspected with:

A. ST elevation only in aVRLeft main/proximal LAD clue.
B. Normal ECG alwaysFalse.
C. ST depression in V1-V2 with posterior lead elevationCorrect.
D. Diffuse PR depression onlyPericarditis clue.

Q5. Right ventricular infarction is important because nitrates can:

A. Reduce preload and cause hypotensionCorrect.
B. Cure RV infarctionNo.
C. Replace reperfusionNo.
D. Increase preloadOpposite.

Q6. Wellens syndrome implies:

A. Benign ECG onlyDangerous.
B. Critical LAD stenosis risk even when pain-freeCorrect.
C. Always inferior MIAnterior precordial T-wave pattern.
D. No need for cardiologyNeeds early invasive evaluation.

Q7. ECG interpretation can be difficult with:

A. Only normal sinus rhythmNo.
B. No comorbid ECG changesNo.
C. LBBB, paced rhythm, LVH, pericarditis, hypothermia, digoxin effectCorrect.
D. Only ankle painNo.

Q8. LBBB STEMI-equivalent concern is strongest with:

A. Random artifactNo.
B. Any discordanceDiscordance can be normal.
C. No symptomsClinical context matters.
D. Concordant ST elevation or excessive discordant elevationCorrect.

Q9. STEMI treatment goal is:

A. Rapid reperfusion by PCI or fibrinolysis when indicatedCorrect.
B. Delay therapy until morningUnsafe.
C. Avoid antiplatelets for allWrong.
D. Ignore ECGWrong.

Q10. Absolute fibrinolytic contraindication includes:

A. Mild headache onlyNo.
B. Any prior intracranial hemorrhageCorrect.
C. Young ageNo.
D. Remote ankle sprainNo.

A. 0 mg alwaysWrong.
B. Only topicalNo.
C. 162-325 mg unless contraindicatedCorrect.
D. Tenecteplase doseDifferent drug.

A. No ACS existsFalse.
B. Fibrinolysis is routineWrong.
C. ECG is irrelevantWrong.
D. Early invasive/medical strategy depends on risk; fibrinolysis is not used for NSTEMICorrect.

B. Height onlyNo.
C. Only oxygen saturationNo.
D. Only chest x-rayNo.

C. No ECGNo.
